one_liner: Korean-standard LSH-256/LSH-512 hash; SUPERCOP's SIMD C code beats BLAKE2 and SHA-3 on long x86 messages.
what_it_does: LSH is a cryptographic hash family from Korea (developed 2014, TTA standard TTAK.KO-12.0276) with 224/256/384/512-bit outputs: LSH-256 uses 32-bit words and 128-byte blocks, LSH-512 uses 64-bit words and 256-byte blocks. The fast code is the NSR (Korea National Security Research Institute, 2016) C implementation shipped in SUPERCOP as crypto_hash/lsh512/avx2 and crypto_hash/lsh256/ssse3 (plus ref, sse2, xop, neon variants). The API is a plain C init/update/final/digest over a context union. It is not a drop-in for anything: lengths are passed in bits, and it produces LSH digests, not SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2 digests.
how_it_is_fast: LSH is an ARX design (add, rotate, xor) with a 16-word chaining value split into left/right halves and a wide-pipe Merkle-Damgard mode. The AVX2 LSH-512 code keeps the whole chaining value in four 256-bit registers and runs 28 steps using vector adds, shift-or rotations, byte-granular rotations via _mm256_shuffle_epi8 and word permutations via _mm256_permute4x64_epi64. Message expansion is vectorized the same way. The SSSE3 LSH-256 code does the same with 128-bit registers and pshufb over 26 steps, and on this CPU it edges out the AVX2 LSH-256 code (5231 vs 5401 cycles for 1536 bytes).
when_to_use: A Korean-standard hash (LSH, TTAK.KO-12.0276) is required and you want the fastest known code for it on x86-64.
Long messages (576 bytes and up) on x86-64 with AVX2 that need a 512-bit digest: on alder LSH-512 runs 2.14 cycles/byte vs SHA-512 5.02 and SHA3-512 11.25.
AMD Zen 4, where the margin is larger: LSH-512 1.72 vs BLAKE2b 3.52 cycles/byte and LSH-256 2.61 vs BLAKE2s 5.53 (hertz, Ryzen 7 7700).
You want code that SUPERCOP lists with constant-time goals: both chosen implementations ship goal-constbranch/goal-constindex files recording a TIMECOP pass.
when_not_to_use: Short messages: at 64 bytes on alder LSH-512 (9.52) and LSH-256 (7.27 cycles/byte) lose to BLAKE2s (4.84), SHA-256 (4.69) and BLAKE3 (3.12). At 8 bytes they cost 60-77 cycles/byte.
When BLAKE3 or SHA-NI SHA-256 is acceptable: both beat LSH on long messages (alder BLAKE3 1.73, SHA-256 2.05; Zen 4 BLAKE3 0.60 cycles/byte).

ARM: on a Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76, supercop-20251222) LSH-512 only ties BLAKE2b (3.76 cycles/byte), LSH-256 is slower than BLAKE2s (6.88 vs 6.22), and SHA-256 with the ARMv8 crypto extensions (2.03) beats both.

You need broad interoperability or a long cryptanalysis record: LSH has few implementations and little outside analysis. A withdrawn 2015 ePrint (2015/494) showed free-start collisions on full LSH because it has no feed-forward, though this is not a practical collision on the standard hash.
You want a packaged, maintained library: the only one found is Crypto++, and SUPERCOP measures its LSH-512 at 2.92x slower than the NSR AVX2 code (11240 vs 3854 cycles for 1536 bytes).

integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler with SSSE3/AVX2 intrinsics (ifdefs also cover MSVC); SUPERCOP's fastest builds used Debian Clang 19.1.7 with -march=native
integration.platforms: x86/amd64 per the architectures file; lsh512/avx2 needs AVX2, lsh256/ssse3 needs SSSE3; separate ref, sse2, xop and neon directories exist
integration.thread_safety: No mutable globals in the source (tables are static const); all state lives in a caller-owned context, so use one context per thread

gotchas: Lengths are in bits: lsh512_update/lsh512_digest take databitlen (SUPERCOP's wrapper passes 8*inlen), so one call covers at most 512 MiB when size_t is 32 bits, and any update after a non-multiple-of-8 bit length returns LSH_ERR_INVALID_DATABITLEN.

Each SUPERCOP directory is a single ISA variant chosen at compile time (LSH_USE_AVX2); there is no CPUID dispatch, and lsh.h declares lsh_init_simd()/lsh_get_simd_type(), which the per-variant lsh-impl.c does not define. Call the lsh512_*/lsh256_* functions from lsh-impl.h and add your own dispatch.

The fastest variant differs by width and CPU. On alder, LSH-256's winner is ssse3, not avx2, and LSH-512's ssse3 code (5206 cycles) is no faster than ref (5203), so benchmark on your target instead of assuming AVX2 is best.

The comments are in Korean. The header says the output buffer must be aligned, but the code uses unaligned stores plus memcpy. lsh512_final wipes the context with a plain memset, which the compiler may remove.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LSH over BLAKE3, blake2_simd, KangarooTwelve (XKCP) or SHA-NI SHA-256 only when LSH itself is mandated, or when you need a 512-bit digest on AVX2 x86 and cannot use BLAKE3. On alder BLAKE3 (1.73) and SHA-256 (2.05) are faster, while LSH-512 (2.14) beats BLAKE2b (3.36) and K12 (2.67).
verified_claims_summary: eBASH on alder (Intel Core i3-12100, Golden Cove, supercop-20260831), long-message medians: LSH-512 (NSR avx2 code, Clang 19.1.7 -O2) 2.14 cycles/byte vs BLAKE2b 3.36 and SHA3-512 11.25, and LSH-256 (ssse3, Clang -Os) 3.13 vs BLAKE2s 5.24 and SHA3-256 5.96. Each row is the fastest implementation+compiler pair SUPERCOP found for that function, picked by the time to hash 1536 bytes (for example 3854 cycles for LSH-512 avx2).
status_note: The NSR code (2016, MIT-style permissive license, about 20-25 KB of C per variant) was added in supercop-20240625 and has not changed in the jedisct1 mirror since; it is small enough to vendor, and SUPERCOP itself is actively released (20260831).
